utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina, et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to you, Mr. Radic, as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to ask a few additional questions in relation to the statement you've given to the Gotovina Defence. In paragraph 24 of that statement, you mention that accommodating the population of Kijevo in Knin and the reconstructions of new houses in Kistanje, which were used to accommodate citizens. Could you tell us a bit more. I think you mentioned it yesterday a few times as well, the reconstruction of houses in Kistanje, when, for whom, how many. Could you give us some details about this, new houses in Kistanje and housing people from Kijevo in Knin. Perhaps we start with Kistanje. Before you answer this question I'd like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave yesterday is still binding. That is, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the construction of apartments or houses in Kistanje is the best example with which we wished to resolve a number of problems that we had at the same time. At the same time, we had expelled Croats, people who were expelled from their homes. Then we had Croats and Bosniaks from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Croats from Serbia, and we also have people who had left their homes in Croatia and for the most part had gone to Serbia. Thus, Serbs. After Oluja, and a large portion of Croatia was liberated, there was a large number in Kistanje --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you there. I'd first like -- I specified my question, when, how many. If we could first go to the facts and then whether it's a good example of A, B, or C and what exactly -- first, I'm interested in knowing the facts of this reconstruction of houses.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kistanje, we built a new part of a settlement with 150 houses, if I remember correctly. Completely new ones in a field. They were completely equipped with all the facilities, infrastructure, and this is where we had the assistance of the government of the United States, through a fund of theirs. They invested in the construction of the water works and the electricity supply. After the houses were completed, we placed people there who were occupying temporarily property that had been abandoned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you when that was. When did you start reconstructing and when were these 150 houses ready.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 150 houses, yes. Well, it's difficult for me to recall the exact date. But it was sometime -- let's say we began a year after Storm. After Storm, right away, we started to prepare the development plans. We were planning a few villages like that. There was a settlement we were planning near Gracac. There was one near Donji Lapac. Unfortunately, this one was never built. And there were several examples I mentioned three large ones with more than 100 houses but there were several smaller ones in different areas. So after Storm, we began to develop the plans but the construction of a village with 150 houses requires a lot of time and a lot of money, of course. As far as can I remember now, I think that we started about a year after Storm with this construction, and then in a year, or a little bit more, well, proof of that and this is something that I remember well, is that the ambassador of the United States at the time was Mr. Montgomery, and so we were distributing keys in a public ceremony to people who were transferred then from temporarily occupied premises so that they could return to Kistanje. I think Kistanje now is a very good example of co-habitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say it's a good example of co-habitation, could you tell us what at this moment, approximately, then the balance is.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know at this point in time. I did go to a sort of celebration there. I was invited to go about three years ago. A Serb was the mayor at the time, and on the basis of that, I conclude that the Serbs were the majority to go and vote. So I assume that the ratio of people living in Kistanje right now is perhaps 50/50. I also know when there are elections, people frequently are organised from Serbia. They come by buses from there in order to vote so perhaps that was a decisive factor. But like I said yesterday I haven't been on this kind of work for the past ten years. I'm no longer doing that work, so now I am just really stating my impressions about the current situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 150 houses approximately were constructed. Do I understand that those who were temporarily housed in Kistanje or from elsewhere, that they moved into those houses?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were transferred to the newly built houses who were previously temporarily placed in abandoned property in Kistanje and its environs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would that be mainly Croats or ...

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part Croats, yes. I think almost over 90 per cent. There was some Bosniaks among them. But from what I remember now, the bulk of them were Croats. For a number of years they had been in privately owned homes of Serbs who had left Croatia. We emptied those houses and freed them up for the Serbs who had left them before to be able to return there. Kistanje is alive again. It's a very nice neighbourhood now with a lot of children. I feel very comfortable there when I go and visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, do I understand -- do you have any data, then, on Serbs, then, returning? And were there programmes for reconstruction of their houses as well? Could you tell us in factual terms what happened there. Because if I hear that people came from buses -- with buss from Serbia to vote, that means that apparently they were not all back in their houses, and if you need buses, then at least a number, a -- not just one or two, but -- could you tell us what, then, happened with the houses that were -- that were left in order to move into the new constructed houses? What happened with the abandoned houses?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said "buses," this referred to a portion of the population. A portion did come back. I will speak about an example that I am familiar with. A family left one house. They had grandfather and grandmother, father and mother, and children. This is really important. It's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Examples are sometimes illustrative; sometimes not illustrative of the overall picture. At this moment, I'm primarily seeking to have information which allows me to have the overall picture rather than one example. Could well be that it is very much representative for the whole of it, but it could also be that it is the exception. So therefore, I'd rather refrain from listening to examples and rather have clear facts, figures, for the overall picture.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All Serbs whose houses were vacated had the option of returning. A number of them during the time that they had spent outside of Croatia managed to get jobs, their children were attending school, let's say somewhere else, in Belgrade, for example, so they had become attached to their work. So a number of people came to Kistanje. Perhaps older people came back. This is why I talked about grandfathers and grandmothers who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the interpreters, could you please slow down. Mr. Misetic also assists me in making the job for the interpreters still bearable. Mr. Radic, you said, "perhaps older people came back." Do you have figures? How many -- how many --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the figures. I didn't say perhaps all of them came back. All of them could have come back and those who wanted to come back did come back. This is not a rule. But taking Kistanje as an example, elderly people who had retirement pensions who had an option of returning but didn't have any children in school somewhere else at that moment, so they didn't have that problem, they returned. Those others who continued to live outside of Croatia would come back when there was a vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, Those who wished to come back did come back. Well, Kistanje was a village with, well, quite a number of inhabitants. Was any research done on whether they wished or not, or is it just that you conclude from the return of some, you can't give us the data, that returned and said they wished to return, that you concluded that those who wished to return did return? Is that -- I mean, what's the basis exactly for your statement? That those who wished to return did return.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm drawing the conclusion on the basis of the fact that everybody had the opportunity to submit an application to return, and for reconstruction, we reconstructed the houses. I don't know what else one could do in order to get people to come back. So I conclude on the basis of administrative procedure that those who wanted to come back did come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say if they're not -- if they did not apply for return, they apparently had no wish to return. Is that, briefly, what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my conclusion. However, there is still the option for these people to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move away from that. Do you know whether the figure of Serbs that, meanwhile, have returned is published anywhere, even if you do not know it by heart? Is there any publication as to the present situation or the situation as it developed over time?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that. Again, I have not been in politics for the past ten years. I'm involved in something completely different now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that leaves, still, the time open from 1999 to 2009, where perhaps would you have had information about the period, 1995/1999.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely, on the basis of what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In your statement, you mentioned the national programme for demographic renewal. Now this Chamber has received a lot of evidence on all kind of programmes and developments. But a programme by this very name, I think we haven't -- we count find it at least. Therefore, I would like to hear from you what that programme, under this name, exactly was. Briefly, please, so that we have a -- that we know where to place it. When was it developed? What did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that is not initially connected to the wartime events. When we established the Croatian state in 1990, there were no longer reasons which had led to the fact that -- that one half of ethnic Croats were in Croatia and half were outside of Croatia. These were most frequently political reasons from Communist times. At the very beginning when we were establishing the Croatian state, and I actually began to do this as early as 1992 when I was minister of education and then I continued as the minister for development and reconstruction. We defined a national programme of demographic renewal which has a few basic principles. The first one, to stimulate population growth. Croatia has a negative population growth. It had it then and it still does. At the time we adopted measures which referred to all the citizens of Croatia. There was no mention of one particular ethnic group, encouraging families with more children. They were child supplements and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked to you to be brief. I do understand that part of the programme was to stimulate families having more children so as to not have a negative population growth. Yes, other parts -- when was the programme developed? When was it put on paper?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The programme was developed from 1992 until 1995 or 1996. I think in 1996 it was adopted by the assembly. 1996. I have to mention three facts at least the first one to stimulate families with more children. The second point was to encourage the settlement of empty swaths of area of Croatia so better population distribution. The third measure was to encourage immigration, the return of Croats who, during the Communist period, left for Germany, Holland, Canada, United States, so that was the main concept of the programme. It was unanimously adopted by the Assembly. It is being applied still today. It was followed by a series of laws on areas of special benefit, then the laws on islands. If the islands were sparsely populated, then laws on hilly terrain. But in any case, these laws applied to all Croatian citizens. I'm just going to mention one more fact. This first group stimulating the birth-rate and families with more children. At the time we had a large number of Roma who wanted to come to Croatia from other countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, at this moment, the Chamber has no further questions for you. Perhaps briefly, Mr. Kay, the Chamber looked at the material yesterday. You provided the 61 pages of which approximately little bit over 20 pages were about de-mining. What the Chamber was seeking was the link between the time-limits set for return, et cetera. We -- I know a lot more about de-mining now, about how to organise it, 2.000 people, ten years, how to pay them, either privately to be done or not. But I didn't find any link to time-limits set for return, and, as a matter of fact, it seemed to very much a very long-term matter. I suggest that if the parties agree that no such thing is found in there, and where I would be surprised if either Prosecution or any Defence team would argue that de-mining was not a major problem. I would expect everyone to accept that after such a war period that de-mining was a huge problem, very expensive problem to -- problem which was very expensive to resolve than it did need a lot of organisation and a lot of -- brought a lot of problems. If the parties would agree on that, then I would leave it at that and not have another 25 or 61 pages in addition into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Within that document, which is why I knew of it, there is an matter right at the end that refers to General Cermak, and that was why I was aware of the subject matter, and it was something that we had in our mind to bar table, because it was relevant for the appointment issue. I don't know whether Your Honour saw that passage and its --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I went through all of the 61 pages. I can't say that I read them line by line, but that is it not what the Chamber was looking for, of course, because the issue was not Mr. Cermak and de-mining.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue was the time-limits set for return, being explained by de-mining concerns. Therefore, if you want to take any action -- but what the Chamber was looking for was not found in there. And may I take it that there is it no disagreement that de-mining of such a large area would take quite a lot of efforts and that there's no dispute about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No dispute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, there was some information in there, such as a large number of people killed, 400 killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I -- I included that in the huge problems when I was talking about what wages to pay -- of course, the beginning was -- the question was 400 people injured or killed, and then it's clear that many were killed. So, therefore, there is apparently no dispute about the seriousness of the situation where there are a lot of mines, and what it takes to deal with that. There are, of course, there is other information as well as where those mines would be found, whether there would be mines where people would normally move around which seems to be -- receive a -- well, a bit of a negative answer. But the Chamber was not looking for the details and the problems of de-mining. If you want to put that on our table, then it should be in a different context and it is not in response to what we were seeking yesterday, that is, documentary corroboration of what the witness told us, that the one month to the three months was also caused by de-mining problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I suppose it's a chicken and egg situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that is all reasoning. That is all reasoning. I no where see anyone saying, Let's stop them for another month because we have still a lot of de-mining to do. The link is -- can be on our minds but is nowhere expressly discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I suppose in that form, but it may have been obvious to the speakers that the problem itself caused by de-mining was part of the very problem that they were dealing with generally with the return. It may not have been expressed as a temporal matter, and I have not seen anything in relation to that, but the actual generality of the problem being, to the speakers minds, being obviously an effecting factor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do see your point. It becomes now more or less argumentative rather than -- and then of course, there could be a lot of arguments, such as if you need 20.000 people for ten years, why would you then extent from one month to three months? And this is all discussed after the moment that those time-limits have been set. We're talking about December 1995. But let's not -- the Chamber, having looked at it, doesn't find a direct answer to its question there, and therefore, will leave it as it is. But, of course, if the parties want to take any other initiative, then you have put already quite a bit on the record, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall I bar table the document? Would that be a convenient route rather than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then certainly not the whole of the document, I would say, because it is just item 2 of the agenda. So that saves another 35 pages. You can consider that. Perhaps Ms. Gustafson would -- would like to respond now or in the future. The Chamber, at this moment, having looked at it, takes no initiative to have it in evidence and waits whatever will be submitted to it. Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to cross-examine, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Gustafson. Ms. Gustafson is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just as a preliminary matter we have, more out of habit than anything, released our cross-examination documents. There was no procedure on that issue indicated by the Chamber, and I don't know if the Chamber has a view on that or not, but I just wanted to indicate that that was something that we had done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We're prepared to do same. I assume that we were going to follow the same procedure that we had previously. So I would just adopt the procedure laid out by Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your good example is followed, Ms. Gustafson -- will be followed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to P462, page 16 of the English and page 25 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Gustafson. I don't know if the parties have lost the LiveNote. I appear to have. I don't know if others have. On my screen. Is this one working?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I've lost it too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We all lost it. Could we work on the other screen for the time being and be informed about a quick restoration of our facilities. Then please proceed. If at any time it causes too big problems, then we'd like to hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, I'd like to go back to the discussion from the 11th of August, 1995 about the Law on the Temporary Takeover of Property that was being discussed at that session. And you looked at that document yesterday. And, again, I'd like to draw your attention to this part of the transcript, where you speak and you say: "Nothing is more important than this, nothing is more important in Croatia today than this, because people are coming, Croats, and I don't know, we don't have a report on this, but I don't know if you know that Vojnic ... has [sic] only 51 inhabitants, today it's a town of 15.000 people, and tomorrow we can fill it up with 15.000, in addition, Lapac has 14 inhabitants, 14 Croats ..." Just stopping there for a moment, when you said Vojnic has only 51 inhabitants and Donji Lapac has only 14 inhabitants, 14 Croats, now, according to the 1991 census, there were precisely 14 ethnic Croats in the town of Donji Lapac and 51 ethnic Croats in the town of Vojnic. And since you used these same figures in your speech, I'd just like to ask you to confirm that you were referring here to the number of ethnic Croats in those places, according to the 1991 census. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so, given that this was a very short time after the Storm, I had no data about members of other ethnicities who may have stayed. I would have guessed that some Serbs had stayed as well, but this was very short time after the Storm, and we did not have any new data on the population there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you said that -- you used the present tense when you said "there are 51 inhabitants in Vojnic and 14 in Donji Lapac," did you mean that the Croats in those towns had been there all along, or did you mean that they had returned to those places after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did declare that I will speak the truth and only the truth, and that it would not be my guess-work so I cannot completely remember what I thought at that time. But I guess that I thought the 51 would now come back, given that now the conditions have been met for them to come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, at this point, you weren't sure if they had come back but you thought those Croats would soon return to those villages. Is that -- is that how I'm to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Because I knew I did receive reports that the buildings, the apartment buildings that were owned either by JNA or some corporations, such as Hrvatske Sume, that they were free and they were intact so it was possible for people to come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could just ask you to try to limit your answers to the precise questions that I have, and if I want more information, I'll ask you, just because I have limited time. Thank you. And also in this speech we looked at this language before in parenthesis. If you look at the screen, it might assist you. In parentheses it says: "(It's more than the number of houses ...)" And you thought that the parentheses indicated that that was somebody else speaking there in the middle of what you were saying? And then right after that you say: "I agree, but it's strategically so important and it's in such a position that we must repair the houses, Gojko, and put Croats there, such is the position of the place." Now you used the word -- the name Gojko there, and it seems to me that it may have been that it was Mr. Susak who said: "It's more than the number of houses," and that's why you said you agreed, but you must -- "... we must repair the houses, Gojko ..."

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Looking at this now, it seems to me that this is not an entire sentence that was spoken by Gojko. So I probably commented or responded to the entire sentence, and this is just one portion of it. I can't remember what the full sentence looked like. It says here, "it's more than the number of houses," but it seems that more was said after this. And I assume I heard the entire sentence. And whoever was making this transcript did not put in the entire sentence. So I do not know what this comment of mine actually refers to.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But do you agree that when you said the name Gojko that you were talking -- that it Mr. Susak who had said something in the middle of what you were saying here?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm almost certain there was no other Gojko at the meeting, apart from Mr. Susak. But I really cannot confirm what was it that he really said, on the basis of what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'd like to concentrate on what you said which was: "I agree but it is strategically so important and it's in such a position that we must repair the houses." Now, you're talking about repairing houses here, and I take it from that that you understood, at least at the time, that there were houses in Donji Lapac that were damaged or destroyed that needed to be repaired so that Croats could move there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt that all the houses that used to belong to Croats before the war were destroyed during the occupation. In the occupied territory, I did not find a single house that used to be owned by a Croat who was expelled that was not burned down. Apart from some of them that were used for other purposes. So in Lapac and in Vojnic there was a small number of Croats prior to the war, but their houses were destroyed whilst they were expelled. So I said let us accommodate them now temporarily in the state-owned apartments but let us immediately start reconstructing their houses so that they can move to their houses rather than stay forever in the properties that were not theirs. This is my understanding of what I said here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But you wanted to move far more than just the 14 Croats who'd lived in Donji Lapac before into Donji Lapac. You wanted to move a large number of Croats there because it was a strategically important location, as you told the Trial Chamber yesterday, right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt about this. As I said yesterday, in Vojnic, Lapac, and Gracac, we had members of the JNA which attacked Croatia, and they left Croatia. So my position was that those apartments which now belonged to the Republic of Croatia should be allocated to members of the Croatian army so that they move there, rather than stay in Zagreb or Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you're not talking here about moving 15.000 HV members into Vojnic. You're talking about moving 15.000 Croats there, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm just trying to explain what I referred to. I also thought about people who worked for the company Hrvatske Sume, Croatian forests. I also thought about teachers, about doctors, a teacher of mathematics from Vojnic left. He used to live in an apartment that was owned by the school and we needed new teachers there. This is what we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now yesterday you were asked about some comments from this meeting that suggested that the Law on Property, the Law on the Temporary Takeover of property would be aimed at guaranteeing persons who were granted property for temporary use, that they would not be expelled if the owner returned, so that the refugees would not return. And you said that some people thought that way, but you thought differently, and you said you always took care of one type and the other type of persons. That was at page 22. By one type and the other type of persons, were you referring there to Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to different types of refugees and displaced persons. Because we always had a number, though be it a small number of persons amongst the refugees and displaced person who were Croats or Bosnians or Serbs. So in no document did we distinguish between persons on the basis of their ethnicity. But even today I tried to explain what we had in mind when we had -- when we said that everybody would be taken care of. So when we offered temporary accommodation for displaced Croats from Bosnia, in Vojnic, we promised them that they would not be kicked out, but we would find other accommodation for them in order to be able to return those houses to -- to refugees who came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic. Again, if you could just try to answer very precisely just the question I'm asking without going into a lot of examples because I just simply don't have time to hear all of these stories.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 18 of this document, in the English, and page 27 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to you look at the second speaker, which again is you. And you say: "We have good houses, intact houses, who do we keep them for? And Mr. Valentic says: "So move them into the houses, and we will provide for that by a law or decree in the coming days?" And Mr. Vrdoljak says: "So they must know that if they move into the house we will not ..." And then Mr. Milas says: "Mr. President, it doesn't even need to be that way. You put everything under the state's sequestration and give guarantees to those inside that nobody will touch them. The state deals with them, and we put that also for these ..." And then somebody says: "We did." And then Mr. Seks says: "President, we did put it into the law, for the second reading, but the people that move into a house have ownership security. They don't want temporary use, they must invest, repair, keep it in order. They want to own it?" And if we go to the next page in the B/C/S, President Tudjman says: "Yes, well, that's clear. It's in our interests too." Now, here, when Mr. Seks refers to ownership, security and that people don't want to temporary use, they want to own it, and President Tudjman responds, Yes, that's clear, that's in our interest too, President Tudjman here is one of those people who thought that the property law should be aimed at guaranteeing that people who are granted these properties for use would not have to leave, if the owner returned; right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecutor asked me that I try to be short, but I assume the answer is always at least twice as long as the question, so your question took several minutes, so I assume that my answer would be a bit longer than that. I hope can agree with this. Yesterday I think I was clear enough. During any discussion, discussion on any topic, including this one, there were different ideas that were voiced. Some people did suggest that we should sequestrate all the property, and that's it. But after this meeting and additional ten meetings we adopted conclusions and the law. And the wording of that law and a the spirit of that law was that the property would be secured that nobody would touch the private property, and that it would be returned to the rightful owners once they come back and once all the necessary conditions are met.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we go to P463 again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, this is the transcript of the meeting from the 22nd of August. Again, you looked at this one yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 in the English and page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And here again you're talking about returning people to the territory. And you say in the third paragraph where it begins: "The second group ..." You say: "The second group is the people who can go to the deserted houses near their own houses. We're having a lot of problems here, they are offering resistance. How should this be done, we simply can't find a way to force our people to do it. Some are eager to go, for example Kijevljani, in most of the cases, accepted to go to Knin. But the people from Banja region won't go to Petrinja. You see Saborski, we had a discussion in Plaski today, and Saborski has got nothing at all, and Plaski is whole. They say I am not going to move twice." And President Tudjman says: "Why would they move twice?" And if we go to the next page you say: "Today over there, and tomorrow to Saborsko. And President Tudjman says: "Well, let them stay there. And you say: "They wouldn't. People are a bit tough about that?" And President Tudjman says: "Wait, is he afraid that he wouldn't be safe? And you say: "He's afraid that he wouldn't be safe, and he's afraid some Serb might come tomorrow. That's one thing. And second, he would rather go to his own house over there. I would look at in some way, but he has to come temporarily. We'll have to come up with some order or something to be a bit hasher with this in order to take the people there." Now, Plaski was in 1991 a largely Serb village, and Saborsko was a largely Croat village; right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And they're both in Ogulin municipality. And here you and President Tudjman are agreeing that the people -- the Croats from Saborsko, which is destroyed, should just stay in the Serb houses in Plaski, and you are complaining that the Croats from Saborsko don't want to do that. They want to return from their homes. Is that a correct understanding of this passage?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of the passage when it says that Saborsko has none, it means that it is destroyed completely. Saborsko is no more. The Serbs leveled it to the ground. We had people from Soborksi accommodated in hotels in Dalmatia, so the dilemma here was whether we would leave them in those hotels in Dalmatia or temporarily find accommodation for them. I emphasise that, temporarily. When we're talking about moving twice, it's a question of then temporarily going to abandoned property, and we would need at least a couple of years to rebuild Saborski. It is unbelievable. The church was raised to the ground, they took the stones of the church away so that it could never be rebuilt. So the people were not very happy, and they were not willing to accept this intermediary step. We needed to get them out of the hotels in order to start off our tourist season. So that's why we wanted them to move to the abandoned property. That's also a way of preserving this property. If it is abandoned too long, it begins to get run down. So they would be moved twice. First moved to a house abandoned by a Serb, and then after their houses are rebuilt, then they would move to their own houses. I believe that this is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's clear that you wanted -- that -- that these people didn't want to move twice; you said that. And President Tudjman says, Well, let them stay there. He's talking about having them stay in the Serb houses in Plaski, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in Plasko, just like in other parts, there is was a small number of homes that were priority property. I keep repeating that and I will do so. A large number of apartments in Plasko were not privately owned, but they were owned by the Croatian state or state institutions. So when the President says, Let them stay there, that's what he is thinking of. Not only in this conversation but in 100 other conversations we always repeated that and implemented that as a principle, private property is inviolable, and we will preserve that. This conversation that we are quoting here is based on my own and the President's noting that we must prevent the destruction and the burning of homes and houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, Plaski was a village of about 2200 people. Do you know how many apartments there were in Plaski versus privately owned homes? Do you have that figure?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. There were both, private houses and apartments. This is data that can be easily checked.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go now to page 4 of the English and page 6 in the B/C/S. And it's at the bottom of the B/C/S where President Tudjman says: "Jure, regarding these returns, we as Croatia should go for inviting people to come back and paying for their trips from Argentina, Australia, et cetera." And if we turn the page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "We should organise some charter flights or ships and tell them they could choose, give them houses, give them land, even take some kind of poll on what they would be interested in. We have to offer them such a possibility, but the state should pay for that." And you say: "It won't cost us a thing." And then President Tudjman says: "That would mean a thousand people, and they would enter the Serb houses, et cetera."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could now go to page 22 of the English and page 33 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And here at the top of the page in the B/C/S and near the middle in the English, it is you speaking again. And the second sentence begins: "Secondly, we have to focus on return of the Croat refugees from Germany, 50.000 them. They still have refugee status over there." And President Tudjman asks if they have region status there. You say: "In Germany, yes they do. The President: "Granted by Germany." If we go to the next page in the English, and you say: "By Germans." And President Tudjman says: "We can go with that. Germans will really gladly offer to organise a planned return." And you say: "We can do that with Germans. I talked to their Minister Scheiber. He even offered us some money for each returnee." The president: "That is all right." You: "Those relations can be strengthened and they can be returned? President: "Jure, create a project now, say, we offer apartments, land in this and this areas, et cetera, come back." And you say: "Okay, we will take care of it in accordance with instruction of the government. They have softened it just a little bit because obviously the legal aspect of that is --" And President Tudjman interrupts and says: "Which one?" And now if I could just ask to you read the next line, because I think there might be a confusion in the translation. If could you read that out in Croatian, where you say, According to present instruction ... Could you read that line, please. It should be near the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will not be given as ownership according to the current proposal but for use so that the world or people wouldn't ... And then the following page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And then if we turn the page in the B/C/S, President Tudjman says: "For how long?" And you say --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For ten years.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you say: "To use it for ten years, which is not bad. During that period man has to live there because someone might want to sell it. After ten years, man would become owner. There is a point in that." Now, you're talking here, when you're talking about what's going on in the government, and you have to soften it because of the legal aspects and it will not be given in ownership but for use, you're referring here to the Law on the Temporary Takeover of Property, is that right, that was being discussed by the government at the time?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conversation has been transcribed quite imprecisely. I see the sentences are not complete. They start in one way. There's -- the conversation started with a Croats from Australia. The President had an idealistic idea about the programme of the democratic renewal -- demographic renewal, which had nothing do with the war, but he worked with it. And then we moved to the topic of the displaced persons from Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'm not asking you about everything you saw here. I had a very specific question about whether when you referred to what was going on in the government, the need to soften it because of the legal aspect, and you referred to the world, and it won't be given in ownership but in use, that a reference to the Law on the Temporary Takeover of Property, that was then being discussed by the government; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I need to interrupt. Mr. President, just in the spirit of clarity, I'm not certain, and I fully comprehend the answer by the witness in the sense that there is some lack of clarity in our transcript, and just for certainly the Chamber's sake, and for our collective sake, if there could be some question by the Chamber as to what may or may not be clear, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Ms. Gustafson is inviting the witness to answer the question rather than to -- What was read to you, what was put to you did Ms. Gustafson, was that about a discussion which -- in which the Law on the Temporary Takeover of Property was discussed. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not only that. At the time, both in the government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... first establish was the discussion about that law. Now whether there was another matter, that's second. Simply, was this a discussion in which - perhaps not exclusively - the Law on the Temporary Takeover of Property was discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was discussed, as well as a series of other documents that we were preparing at the time. At the time I was preparing the programme of return, the principles of return, the reconstruction programme. A whole range of projects, not only that one law. But, of course, that law was on the agenda as well. I cannot say. I would lie if I were to say that at that point in time President Tudjman and I were discussing exclusively that document at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the portions put to you by Ms. Gustafson were primarily focussing on that law. Is that -- that's apparently what Ms. Gustafson would like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot be sure. I cannot confirm that from this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you said, According to present instruction, it won't be given in ownership but in use, and you refer to the world, are you referring to the concern that the international community would not accept a law that simply transferred the ownership of Serb's property to either the government or to Croats? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's beyond dispute that the international community would not accept that, but it is also indisputable that we would not adopt anything like that in that form. So it was not only just a question of the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are repeatedly explaining what apparently you want to explain. Ms. Gustafson simply asked you whether the reference to the world was a reference to the international community, which might not accept. Now, whether you had other reasons to do the same thing, that's not what Ms. Gustafson is asking you. Ms. Gustafson is asking you when you used those words, whether you had with the world on your mind the international community which, as you testified, would not have accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Radic, also in this passage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Oh, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We still need an answer. You said also -- but you would agree that the reference to the world was the reference to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I agree. The international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Radic, when you said to President Tudjman that you had to focus on the return of the Croat refugees from Germany, 50.000 of them, were those Bosnian Croat refugees you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly they were Croats from Croatia. A certain proportion were Croats from Bosnia. But mostly this was about Croats from Croatia. For example, from Slunj which was at the centre of these event, they went to Germany during the war, found temporary work there. At the time, I had a meeting with the German minister for development who informed me that a large number of people came and through their friends, family, who were in Germany, and received refugee status in Germany. But it's hard to see which Croat actually came from Bosnia to Croatia, and then from Croatia went to Germany. So it is hard to tell exactly which Croats they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you're not sure. Now, the Law on the Temporary Takeover of Property was discussed, as we saw, after Operation Storm. But the procedure for this law was initiated quite a bit before Storm, and it was contemplated that such a law would be passed several months before Operation Storm. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Before Storm, there was Flash, we had liberated the area of Western Slavonia a few months before Storm. There was a similar situation, the scale of which was larger after Storm, actually, occurred in Western Slavonia after Flash operation. And this was in May. Storm was in May --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and Flash was in June.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, again, try to keep your answers as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 846, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, this is a session of the VONS held on the 30th of June, 1995. And the main subject discussed at this meeting is a visit by President Tudjman and other state representatives to Australia and New Zealand, and here discussed measures aimed at bringing Croatian emigres to live and settle in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 7 of the English and page 15 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, here you're speaking and -- about something like ten lines down, you say: "The main thing is how to deal with that man there, the Croat who is there, how to make possibilities to bring at least some of them here, with the goal to bring as many ... here as we can. It is kind of a coincidence that we will discuss it today in parliament, probably it will be scheduled for today. If not, it will be on the very next day, the law that we have discussed about for a long time, at urgent procedure, to talk about Serb's houses and cottages and Croatian state will take over the ownership over these objects in certain way. "On government session, we have discussed it yesterday and the day before in ... cabinet, we will present the resolutions - how to provide the operational plan for using these objects. Well, we are talking about several dozens of thousand houses, several dozens of thousand houses, if we are talking about cottages, if we are talking about deserted houses, and now in this action ... Flash but many more."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "We really have to create the most serious strategy how to deal with these problems. Probably according to international law, it would be some temporary solutions, but temporary which will under such circumstances, and as time goes by, will become permanent, and we will be" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "And we will be able to bring our people back, people that have been forced out from Bosnia, but many more we are mentioning today, who will come back from Australia. So, it is not related only to houses, we are talking about properties, so starting today, after the implementation of that law, we have the opportunity to provide complete properties to be used temporarily. We have to work on that, on the government session also and in the inner cabinet within the government's department [sic]. We have to discuss the issues, to avoid this operation becoming automatically a goal at international level, but to present it as a positive step forward." Now, here you're talking about the law that eventually became the Law on the Temporary Takeover of Property, and you discuss the fact that this law would be a way to bring Bosnian Croats and Croats from the diaspora into Croatia, that they would settle in these houses that are taken over, the property of Serbs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your question, you left out just one word, which I have used at least 20 times in this brief passage, and that is the word "temporary." Yes, so it all stands, we will take over that property. By law we will preserve it. It will still remain private property if it was private property at first, and then it would be given for temporary use. So that word "temporary" is the key word here. This was accepted in the law and that is the form in which the law was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, you said, Temporary, which will under such circumstances, and as time goes by, will become permanent. So what you mean here is that a Croat from Australia will come to Croatia, settle into a property owned by a Serb. It will initially be labelled a temporary situation, but it will become permanent, and that Croat will say in that house. That's what you mean here; right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They will remain permanently in Croatia. As to whether it would be in that house or some other house, time would show. Today -- up to now time has shown that a number of Serbs exchanged or sold their houses. No person had their property confiscated. There was always an exchange or a sale that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And earlier you had referred --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could tender 65 ter 846.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned exhibit number P2711. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2711 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm about to move to another topic, so if the Chamber prefers, we can take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you don't think that you deal with it in the next five minutes, then it's best to take the break now. Will take a break and resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, yesterday you were asked by the Chamber whether you could point to a time between August 1995 and December 1996 when there was some general call to inhabit the country, whether of Croat or Serb ethnicity. And in your answer you referred to the Law on Areas of Special State Interest which provided certain incentives such as larger salaries. And you said: "There is not a single article in it which would actually identify people according to their ethnic backgrounds. Simply this was an attempt to revitalize these regions." And that was at page 40 of yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to P2698 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, a document is about to come up on your screen. And I'd like to you confirm that this law called the Law on Areas of Special State Concern, was the one that you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the one I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 7 and page 4 in the B/C/S, where we could see Article 7 of this law.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And paragraph 2 of Article 7, near the bottom of the page, sets out the categories of population that will be stimulated in the areas of special state concern. And the first you can see is: "Citizens" -- Croatian citizens who have various expert professions and occupations. The second is citizens who are unemployed or have no accommodation. And if we turn the page in the B/C/S, the third category is Croatian emigres, returnees from abroad. And the fourth category is those Croats who have been expelled from Serbia and Montenegro, as well as Croats who were expelled from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So when you said yesterday that there wasn't a single article in this law which would identify people according to their ethnic background, there actually were a couple of provisions in this law that identified people according to their ethnic background; right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could just see the previous page once again, in Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Certainly. If we can go back, please.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Article 7 describes the incentive measures for settlement, and here it says citizens of the Republic of Croatia. This is all the citizens of the Republic of Croatia. And then, thereafter, it also talks about settlement of those people who may not be citizens of the Republic of Croatia yet. But, here you can see that it describes settlement of this area, and prior to this, it describes incentive measures for all the citizens of the Republic of Croatia. So certainly there is no exclusion provision of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, this law was neither intended -- it was not intended to either encourage or even allow Croatian Serbs to return to these areas. This was about stimulating the settlement of Croats into these areas, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Quite the contrary. I have to say I disagree with you. My position is quite the contrary. The goal of this law was for all the citizens of the Republic of Croatia - and this is what the first paragraph of this article says - citizens of the Republic of Croatia, experts of all the professions and occupations who can contribute to the economic development of the area. So we are talking about all the citizens of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Why doesn't it say, then, all the citizens of the Republic of Croatia? Because it says citizens of the Republic of Croatia, experts of various professions and occupations. And then it says: "Citizens of the Republic of Croatia - those who are unemployed or those with no accommodation." Those are two very specific categories of Croatian citizens. And then the rest of the article describes categories of ethnic Croats.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All other articles of this law talk about returnees. So everybody who used to live in that region before. And on top of that, in this Article 7, we also talked about settling of those people who did not live in that area before but they were unoccupied at the time, unemployed, or they were of professions that were relevant for that region at the time. But prior to this, we listed all those who might come back and benefit from this law. So Article 7 simply describes one segment, one segment of people who might come and settle there in addition, and they did not live there before. But even in this Article, paragraph 1, says: "Citizens of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you please refer me to the provision of this law that talks about returning the people who used to live in that region before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I think it might be easier if the witness is given a hardcopy in Croatian so he can review. I don't know how long the actual law is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson will provide him with it. And if the witness from his recollection can't answer the question, then he will have an opportunity to look at that it during the break, the next break, and then ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember this law well and all the previous articles. Even here you can see that some settlements are listed, in which life as such will be stimulated. So this is the law that deals with all the people who live in this area who can come back, who are citizens of the Republic of Croatia, and who are entitled to incentives. If you allow me a second, I might find a provision.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I have very limited time. So I'm going ask you to put the law away for now, you can look at it in the break, and I'm going move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could please go to 65 ter 7574.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me can I answer with one single sentence. I found the answer to your previous question, if Your Honours' allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the one single sentence is granted. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Article 1 of this act, which says: "This act determines the areas of the Republic of Croatia in which reconstruction and development will be incentivised." So this is Article 1 of this act. And Article 2 says: "These areas are determined in order to remove the consequences of the war and to accelerate the return of refugees and displaced persons." We used to describe Croats who moved away as displaced persons, as refugees referred to Serbs. So in the first two Articles, have you the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, refugees there did not refer to Serbs, did it? That referred to refugees from Bosnia because at this time Croatia didn't consider Croatian Serbs living outside of Croatia to be refugees, did they?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were refugees equally, and refugees were also Serbs from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If you could look at the document on your screen now. This is a report from the HINA news agency dated the 4th May, 1996, right around the time that this law was passed. And if you could look at where the text after the word "ZAGREB" in all capital letters. "At today's press conference, deputy prime minister and minister of Development and Reconstruction, Jure Radic, spoke about a bill on areas of special state care in which allotting of houses, apartments, and land for agriculture, tax exemptions, and custom privileges, and higher wages are stimulating measures. It is one of the strategic laws of long-term importance, since we are correcting historical injustice, the minister remarked and mentioned that in 1880, 1217 inhabitants lived in Knin, 613 of them Croats, and 435 Serbs. But in 1991 there were 12.331 inhabitants, 1660 of them Croats, and 9.867 Serbs. He mentioned examples of a complete disappearance of some Croatian settlements, and he stressed that from the demographic, economic, and other points of view, the law covers the whole territory of the Croatian state, although it is specifically related to two groups of areas: Areas next to the state border, which were occupied until 1995, and their centre is not more than 15 kilometres far from the state borders [sic]; and areas which were occupied and do not belong in the first group." Now, first -- do you recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. Mr. President, we had a 66(B) from the Office of the Prosecutor concerning a variety of documents, and we did receive some disclosure, but we never, I do not believe, received this from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I can't tell you off the top of my head. I can look into it. But I don't think this falls under the request. Because I don't believe it falls into any of the categories that were requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well it certainly does fall into the statements of the media which was requested and was disclosed in other instances by the OTP, so certainly it falls into the same category.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, no that wasn't the request. The request was statements that refer to particular topics, none of which are discussed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's, at this moment, the document is there. What to do, let's not spend, at this moment, in court, time on whether there was any violation of any obligation by one of the parties at this moment. Not to say that we'll not look into the matter, but not fully litigate it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, the -- my first question is, do you recall giving this statement to the press; and is this report accurate, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not remember that, and having read this now, I can already see that this news report is rather imprecise, as the news reports usually are. But, at that time, on a daily basis, you had a dozen of different information reported in the press concerning our work. So I do not recall this particular instance precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it gives quite specific and precise numbers of people who lived in Knin in 1880 versus 1991, and they attribute that information to you. Looking at it now, are any of those figures incorrect, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that they are incorrect. But I can neither confirm these numbers nor deny them. I believe that they do reflect the situation as it was 100 years ago and 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you have no reason to doubt that you did provide these figures as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, we have two different matters. First, whether the -- the witness says, I don't remember this interview or this statement to the press. And then he said, I have no reasons to doubt the numbers. And then in the next question you say, Therefore you have no doubt that you gave these numbers. That is mixing up two things. So you should first specifically ask the witness, Did you ever, in a press conference, make a comparison between ethnic composition in 1880 and 1995. I mean, you say, I don't remember. You say it is imprecise. Did you ever compare, in terms of numbers, the ethnic composition of the population of Knin in 1880 with the composition in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- please proceed, Ms. Gustafson. This link was missing in your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do you recall referring to this law as a strategic law aimed at correcting a historical injustice?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember any such details that I may have said during the press conference. In that period that I was a minister, I probably held about 1000 different press conferences, but, generally speaking, as a rule, journalists provided their impressions, and I never read them afterwards. At least 50 per cent of all the news reports were very imprecise. I used to have -- and I still have a rather negative experience with journalists, and I would never take any news report as a trustworthy document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you said you couldn't remember any such details. Do you have any specific reason to doubt that you referred to this law on this occasion as aimed at correcting a historical injustice?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can neither doubt it or not. I simply do not remember the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could I tender this document, 65 ter 7574.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President we do have an objection to it, so if the Chamber would MFI it at this point, and we can address the 66(B) issue because we pulled up a message that we sent to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be MFI'd. Mr. Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2712. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps the status of marked for identification. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to 65 ter 7573, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, this is another press report from about a year later, 16 April 1997, from Vjesnik. And if you could look at the far left hand column and the first full paragraph there under the name, I believe, of the author, Miroslava Rozankovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could move it over -- there is some text cut off on the left-hand side in the B/C/S, and perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the title of this article is: In May another offer to settle abandoned Croatian areas. And the first paragraph says: "Some 50.000 Croats expelled from BiH, Vojvodina, Srijem, and Kosovo have so far been accommodated in the areas of special state concern. From Kostajnica to Glina and Gvozd on one side; and on the other from Benkovac, Obrovac, and Karin, across Northern Dalmatia to Knin where there are 30 babies born a month. Represented by the minister of development and reconstruction, Dr. Jure Radic, Croatia stated that it would readily accept its every expelled citizen, as it is obliged to do according to the constitution. This state is ready to accept also Croats expelled from the BiH, unless they have the possibility to return to their homes, because they are also Croatian citizens. As a matter of fact, Croatia has already proved it when, at one point, without any help from abroad, it managed to accommodate as many as half a million refugees and expellees. Croatia is not afraid of Croats, it welcomes every Croat, and we are all obliged to help in this matter." And then it says those were the words of Minister of Reconstruction and Development, Mr. Jure Radic. Now, this Article written about a year after that law was passed, states that some 50.000 Croats from Bosnia and Serbia had been accommodated in areas of special state concern. And is -- my question is, is that information accurate, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't give any precise numbers, but I believe that this is right. And nearly everything that is stated here, I would restate today again.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you agree with the passage that I read out and have no reason to doubt that you said those words at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe this is correct. There were about 50.000 people expelled from Bosnia and Herzegovina who could not return to their homes. Therefore, we provided them with properties that were, for the most part, state owned, so that they could live there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, this article doesn't say anything about Serbs from the area returning to their homes. There's just a passage at the end about how Serbs will sell their property in Croatia. And my question for you is: Can you -- are you able to tell the Chamber specifically how -- or even approximately how many Croatian Serbs had returned to this area between May 1996, when this law was passed, and April 1997, when you gave this statement?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even here, you warned me on a couple of occasions that I shouldn't describe the entire situation in every single answer I give. So probably here, in this particular interview or press conference I gave statement about the people who came from Bosnia and Herzegovina, who were expelled from Bosnia and Herzegovina. But, at this point, I can say that in that period of time you referred to the number of Serbs who returned was very small. Certainly much smaller than the 50.000 Croats who came there. Later on, the numbers changed; but at that time, that number was very small, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could I tender this document, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2713. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2713 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go to P464, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, the document that's about to come up on your screen is a transcript of a meeting you had with President Tudjman on the 23rd of August, 1995. And that's one day after the meeting you had, on the 22nd of August, that you looked at yesterday, the one where you had the map. And this is a meeting that President Tudjman held with certain military officials, and you attended it, and it related to demographics and the placement of various military facilities and military units. And I'd like to go to page 2 in both languages, please. And this is President Tudjman speaking here, part way down this first paragraph, after the pause, three dots in English he says: "It may well be, if we find a proper way for one of the most effective components of state policy to solve our essential problem today, and that is Croatia's demographic situation. That is why I asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Development and Reconstruction, Dr. Radic, to come to this meeting and talk about the demographic situation in Croatia today." And then a few lines down, he says: "On the other hand, in order to ... as soon as possible - today it is not so much a matter of changing the kind of population as of populating certain areas, certain places, certain areas." And then he asks you to talk about the situation. And if we move down to the bottom of the page, you thank the President. And then you say: "I think that all of us know that after the liberation of Croatia the biggest problem in Croatia is Croatian man. Simply put, for several reasons there are fewer and fewer Croats every day. One reason is that many people have emigrated or were forced out in the past for political or economic reasons." Now, just pausing there for a moment, when you say there's fewer Croats every day and you talk about people emigrating or being forced out in the past, is that another reference to the historical injustice that has caused a -- that caused a reduction in the number of Croats over the past, say, 100 years?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they are mentioned, especially during Communist rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page. And this is you speaking again, and about six lines down there's a sentence that begins: "But the worst part of this very, very" -- "the worst part of this," sorry, "is a very, very unfavorable distribution of population, that is, of the population that we do have. That is why we have areas that are almost completely empty in the Croatian territory, where there are almost no Croats." And then a few lines further down there's a sentence that begins: "Today ..." And you say: "Today we have analysed in detail the liberated territory and determined the sequence of demographic priorities, that is, the sequence of the territories that are strategically important for Croatia according to where there are no Croats, so that we might try in various ways to populate these areas. In this sequence, the critical territory is the one in the narrowest part of Croatia where the planners in Belgrade and elsewhere wanted Croatia to be bisected. Therefore, from our point of view, the priority areas in terms of building up the population includes the former municipalities of Vrginmost, Vojnic, and part of Karlovac municipality. That is the territory of Petrova Gora and around that mountain. In these three municipalities before the war, here on this map, where it is marked bright red, this is where only 4.259 Croats lived, while there were 26.298 Serbs. This then is an almost completely empty territory and the number one national priority is to populate this territory with Croats and attempt everything possible to create a balance." My first question, Mr. Radic, is: When you refer to the number of Croats living in this area around Petrova Gora and the number of Serbs, those are the numbers from the 1991 -- or based on the 1991 census. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And where you say here that -- that this is the -- this is a critical territory in the narrowest part of Croatia where the planners in Belgrade and elsewhere wanted Croatia to be cut, and therefore from our point of view, the priority areas are the municipalities of Vrginmost, Vojnic, and Karlovac, here you are explaining the need to fill up these strategically important areas with Croats as a way to protect Croatia from the strategic threat that you talk about here, the threat of being cut. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. This is an area -- you were reading, and then you stopped before a key sentence, which states that this was a consequence, the fact that this space is empty, of Greater Serbia-conceived policies, while it was deliberately preparing the aggression, this space was emptied. So when we look at today's structure of Croatia, perhaps it would be a little bit of an anticipating to foresee that all the people would return to their houses. There are too few inhabitants. Any inhabitants -- this is being said at a military session. And this was the thinking while thinking of establishing military units, the thinking was to place a military unit in to one of those areas. We had empty areas, empty accommodation, so it was necessary to bring people from there. Not only from the sentences but from the context you can see that it would be simple to bring the Croatian Army there tomorrow and accommodate them in those apartments, which are empty, and were previously in the possession of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
