utterances.text: Just now you mention the fact that there were too few inhabitants. But in this passage, you focus on the fact that there were only 4.259 Croats and you say: "The number one national priority is to populate this territory with Croats." Here you're not talking about inhabitants in general. You're talking about moving Croats into these areas, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always have to stay in the context of the story. Why I would talk to the military leadership about the return of the Serbs? I spoke about that in a different place. I spoke about that to the government. Each type of meeting has its own topic. Here we're talking about locating military units. Why we would put them in Zagreb? I said let's go to Vojnic, where we have enough space and the area is empty. We would need -- when talking about education, we would say, Let's send teachers there is. When we're talking about doctors, then we would talk about a specific location where you would need to send doctors. So, depending on the type of meeting, that would be the topic that would be discussed, as appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, it was discussed about moving certain military facilities into these areas, but that was a way to bring Croats into those areas to fulfil the larger goal. And I'd like to go back a page, again, to where -- in this document, to where President Tudjman says, near the end of his speech, after he says, "Today it is not so much a matter in the change of the kind of population as of populating certain areas," he says: "This means, if you put large commands, training institutions, and so on, in certain places, dozens and hundreds of people will go there who will have to have families and so on, and immediately the situation, the life, and so on, will be different." President Tudjman here is talking about moving military units and institutions into these areas as a means to fulfill the larger goal of populating these areas with Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't find that here, what you were reading here. I could not follow it on my page as having the President say it in quite that way. He said the opposite. Not that we -- not that we're having demographic problems now, but we don't have people anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, it's the last few lines of the second-last paragraph, where President Tudjman is still speaking, right in the middle of the page. But I'm not interested in pursuing this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I would ask that the witness be allowed to look at that, get himself oriented on this page, and answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the witness is entitled to answer the question. Ms. Gustafson, could you guide him to where he may find the line --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Have you found -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Have you found the passage?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking about it, it says today it is not so much a matter of changing the kind of population as of populating certain places. So we're not talking so much about changing the population but of populating certain places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to give the interpreters the opportunity to translate the words you and the others are speaking. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Radic, because, right now, in this area, there was essentially nobody. And as you said, the number one national priority was to populate this territory with Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go back again to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first priority was populating the area. At first it was not realistic to expect the displaced Serbs to return within two, three, or five days. And since this was so, it was necessary to bring those people, those citizens that we did have available, so that the area is populated. And the most important thing, the military units, some 10 kilometres away from across the border, were still there where the war had not been ended. Mladic was still operating with his military units, only some 10 kilometres away, across the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President, there is a phrase that the witness continues to use that I think -- he may want to repeat just so we're sure on the interpretation of the phrase when the -- the reference in page 50, line 23, "not realistic to expect the ..." something Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you -- I read part of your answer and then ask you to repeat again what you then said. You said: "The first priority was populating the area. At first it was not realistic to expect ..." And then you were talking about apparently persons returning. Could you repeat, what persons you refer to? So not realistic to expect the ... to return.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation], first of all, it's not realistic to expect that the Serbs who had lived in that area and who left the area from the time of Storm to return in the short-term. It is not realistic to expect some of them to return at all. Which ones? Those who had taken part in the armed aggression against Croatia, members of the Yugoslav People's Army, members of the paramilitary units, and so on and so forth. So our estimates and the estimates of the international community were that it was not realistic that such people would return. This is what is being said in this sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we are primarily verifying the translation and properly understand what you said. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, back to what you said about this bright red area on the map that you appear to have again at this meeting. You talk about the territory of Petrova Gora, which includes the former municipalities of Vrginmost, Vojnic, and part of Karlovac, and you say this is the part marked bright red. Now, this is the part of the territory where, the day before, you and President Tudjman, had talked about not even 10 percent of Serbs being there ever again; right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drew yesterday on the map the area that I had shown to President Tudjman when we were talking about the idea of not having more than 10 percent of Serbs in the future. So I'm staying on the map that I showed yesterday. At the meeting of the military leadership the map was evidently more precise than the one that we used during our internal conversation the day before. So this more precise map, I think the area covered was not identical. What we're talking about here is a smaller part of larger area. The day before with President Tudjman, I talked about the area between Krupe and Una. And here actually we're talking about two municipalities, the municipality of Vojnic and Vrginmost, for which we do state quite precise figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, what Ms. Gustafson asked you is whether these municipalities, that -- whether that was part of the territory where you and President Tudjman had talked about in the context of the, not even 10 per cent. From a very long answer, I take it that a simple "yes" would give us the information Ms. Gustafson is seeking. Because in a rather long explanation, you say it was a smaller part, that was already included in the question; and it was about the territory you and President Tudjman talked about, which was already in the question as well. So a simple "yes" would have given us, perhaps, less detailed information but would certainly have answered the question, because summarizing what you said, it is a yes, if you carefully look at the question. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could go to the next page, please, of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is you speaking again, Mr. Radic. And you say: "This is a critical point. The area below this, the Slunj area where Croats should be returned is on the same crisis level. It is also quite empty but luckily, there were no Serbs there or there were very few. Therefore, from our point of view, this territory is on the same level, this red and blue area in the narrowest part of Croatia where Croatia was completely cut." Now when you say "luckily there were no Serbs or very few Serbs there," that's a reference to the fact that it will be easier to populate this part of the territory with Croats, because there were very few Serbs there before.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I said "luckily," luckily in this area there were fewer aggressors. We're talking about a couple of days after Storm. Colloquially speaking, when we're talking about Serbs, at least a half of them were aggressors in Croatia, so fortunately there weren't many such people in Slunj. Unfortunately, though, Slunj was completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, unlike the areas of Vrginmost and Vojnic, which were predominantly Serb in 1991, Slunj was - I'm looking now - about 64 per cent Croat and about 29 per cent Serb in 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so. I have no reason to doubt that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And can you tell me specifically the circumstances you're referring to that caused you to conclude that there were fewer aggressors in this area? Specifically.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It wasn't the Croats who were attacking Croatia. There was a small number -- I mean, I don't understand what the point of your question is. I didn't understand, of course, that the Croats from Slunj were not attacking Croatia. The Serbs occupied Slunj and completely destroyed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I asked you whether, when you said there were fewer Croats in Slunj -- or, sorry, fewer Serbs or very few Serbs in Slunj, if that was a reference to the ethnic breakdown of Slunj, essentially, and you said, No, there were more aggressors there. And I would like to ask you specifically the circumstances you were talking about that caused you to conclude there were more aggressors there.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be some confusion. I do understand the witness to say, that if it's -- if you're lucky that there are not many Serbs, that since the witness told us that the Serbs were the aggressors, that means that there are less aggressors as well. And to that extent, put Serbs on an equal footing with -- with aggressors. Now, if Serbs are the aggressors, that's at least how I understand it, that's it's not primarily on the basis of ethnicity that you are happy that there are less, but since this ethnicity appeared to be the aggressors, that you were happy with less aggressors. It's a bit -- perhaps a bit of a semantic issue. But this is how I understood your testimony, and this is also how I understood your lack of understanding of the follow-up question. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, moving on to the next paragraph on this page you say: "The next priority, the third on the scale, depending on whether we should include into our considerations the territory of Herceg-Bosna, or Bosnia and Herzegovina ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "... the third priority, the third on the scale, depending on whether we should consider the territories of Herceg-Bosna and Bosnia and Herzegovina. It could be rotated more or less towards Croatia's depth. "Therefore, if the liberated territory around Livanjsko Polje, Glamoc, Kupres, Grahovo, and Drvar is populated with Croats in the future, then the area around Knin would become of smaller significance." Now, Mr. Radic, here you're explaining that if the areas in Bosnia that border on the Knin region can be populated with Croats, then that helps to protect the areas around Knin, because it would be further into the depth of Croatian-populated territory. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, that area was freed by the Croatian Defence Council and in the strategic sense of looking at Croatia there were no major defence threats if Croats were on the other side of the border. As opposite to the other border where Serbs were on the other side of the border and where a serious war was still continuing. So this is a conversation before the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this part of Bosnia that you refer to - Glamoc, Kupres, Grahovo, and Drvar - that in 1991 that was an area with a heavy majority of Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But generally speaking the population there was very sparse. And similar to the situation in Croatia, many of them were members of the Yugoslav People's Army in these areas next to the border.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And by this point, in August of 1995, most of the Serbs from those municipalities had left, in connection with their liberation by Croatian forces and Bosnian Muslim forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The situation was similar to that in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P463 now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Radic, we're going back to the conversation you had the day before with President Tudjman, the one that you looked at yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 35 of the English, and page 55 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, here, Mr. Radic, at the top of the page, you're talking to the President. And you say: "You did a perfect job, history will be the judge of that. Still, the coming period is very important. You have to prepare Croatia for the future time, that is the main task. Croatia has to avoid facing the situation like Yugoslavia did after ..." And then it trails off. And you continue: "That often happens after the period characterised by the strong personalities. That is very important. We have to create conditions to prevent Croats from ..." and it trails off again. And you say: "It was a beautiful picture to see the people from Varazdin and Split entering ... Knin together. On the one wall in Kupres, the message, 'Cedo, you will not come back' can be seen. Our future has to be built on such things ..." Now, the name Cedo, short for Cedomir, is a typical Serb name; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think the witness has also picked up on it, but there is now a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if there is something that the witness picked up, then we'll invite him, rather than you at this moment. Yes, a question was put to you, and is there anything --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two remarks on my behalf. This may be a mistake where it says "Kupres" because prior to that you can see on a wall in Knin. And I said that the people from Varazdin and Split came together in Knin, and then in Knin on one wall it says, "Cedo, will not come back." But the point I wanted to make to the President was that Croats from different areas were together, and it is actually in a dialect, "you will not come back," in a dialect of Zagorje, a region in Croatia. So I said here, Even Croats from Zagorje, and one of the accused here are from Zagorje, so they came to Knin together with people from Split. So we are talking about unity of different areas of Croatia. This is what my point was. I wanted to underline that people from Varazdin who speak in Kajkavian dialect of Croatian wrote on the wall, "Cedo you will not come back," [B/C/S spoken], but this is in the dialect; that is my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, he has explained what I was going to say, so that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I took it that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm confused here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So am I, a bit. Could you perhaps, then, clearly explain what those words, "Cedo you will not come back," mean exactly. Who or what is Cedo? And could you please better explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cedo meant Chetnik. So you can translate it into, "Chetnik, you will not come back." You will not return. So colloquially speaking the word "Cedo" was used to designate Chetnik. So this was the worst possible version of occupier of Croatia. But as I said, the point of this conversation I had with the President was for me to explain to him that the units that came to Knin were not only for -- from Dalmatia, but in the defence of Croatia we had a unity of all the Croatian areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that, "Cedo, you will not come back," is language which could be understood in various ways? Occupier, don't come back; or Chetniks - that is a derogatory word for people of a certain ethnicity - don't come back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, whoever read this message understood this in one single way, and this was, Occupier, you will not return. So there were different names for Serbs, but if you said "Cedo," it -- it meant Chetnik. It is similar in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand, but you say it would be understood by everyone as "occupier." I asked you whether you would agree with me that the language in itself, not referring to occupier but to Chetniks, could also be understood as a reference to Serb population. Not to say that -- you say what you intended to say, but I'm asking whether you agree with me that the language in itself is not unambiguous.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is hard to say. We would have to analyse it more in depth. Possibly there could have been people who could understood it in different ways; there, I agree with you. But the majority of people at that time in Croatia would understood it as referring strictly to the occupiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday you told us that it was difficult for you to tell us what was on other people's mind. But here you can tell us what -- I'm not arguing about this, but -- Yes, please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go to page 24 of the English and page 36 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, this is a portion of the transcript where you and President Tudjman talk about the division of Bosnia. And you say -- and this is at the top in the B/C/S and in the middle in the English: "Look, we can get Kupres back. It is unreasonable that they do not want to return but still stay in the hotels. They say that some hill above them has not been liberated yet. They call it Demirovac, which is directly above Kupres. As I was told, there were Serb villages in this area, which are now being settled by the Muslims. Our people refuse that. We have to find a way to return people over there. Kupres, it is not strategically my priority, but this hinterland of Dubrovnik, that is also important question. We have to keep Stolac Croat, probably Trebinje if ..." And then you say: "This is the priority, just as Petrova Gora as banovina." And President Tudjman says: "If we could do something with Jajce." And you say: "That will be difficult with the Muslims." And President Tudjman says: "The best solution is to make a deal with Muslims. On the other hand, our strategy has to focus on keeping them close to us and convert them to Croats gradually. That will be very difficult, but not as with Serbs today, because Serbs had Belgrade and power; they won't." Now, first of all, you're describing that you're having trouble moving the Croats from Kupres back to Kupres, because there are Muslims living in areas where Serbs used to live, and the Croats from Kupres don't want to move back for that reason. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kupres was majority populated the by Croats prior to the war, and an I knew a lot about this situation because they spent their refugee years in Baska Voda, which is my place of birth. So I talked to them on many occasions, and I said to them as soon as the conditions are met, please go back home. And then they said they didn't want to go back because the Demirovac was still occupied by Serbs. Serbs fired still on Kupres from Demirovac, and this is what they said. They said this is why we are staying still in hotels in Baska Voda. So I told the president here, Let us do something about this because their houses are empty, and they should be able to go back. Why stay in the hotels?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, earlier you said that the Serb population had left this area, and it had been liberated. And in this passage, you say that: "There are Serb villages which are now being settled by Muslims and our people refuse that."

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "our people do not want to," I meant our people do not want to go back to their homes. Not settle other areas. They do not need other areas since they have their own homes there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, here, again -- or here President Tudjman refers to the strategy of keeping Muslims close and gradually converting them to Croats. And he contrasts that with the Serbs who had Belgrade and power.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just ask that the translation of that word has been translated and "converts to Croats." But there may be a challenge to that. And if we look in the original, perhaps the witness can explain what he think that is that means.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could just read that sentence out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If could you guide the witness then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what the President meant. He spoke about this often. He said that Muslims in Bosnia were a strategic partner to Croats. And when he said "to Croatise them," he meant to make them more European so that the Muslims in Bosnia, together with Croats, should become elements of the western civilisation. This is what I think I can say to make it as simple as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And If you could also just read that sentence out, the second sentence of President Tudjman's speech that begins, "On the other hand ..."

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "That will be very difficult. They will not be easy, but it will be an easier problem than it is -- than the Serbs are to today because the Serbs had Belgrade and power, and these will not have." Do you want me to comment on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that when you refer to the second sentence that it is a sentence which may not be the second sentence in Croatian, because at least I do see a full stop after -- in the beginning. You are invited to read where it says: "On the other hand, our strategy has to focus ..." Could you please read that portion slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, so the second half of the first sentence which says: "But strategically we have to count on the fact that there is no other way but to carry the Muslims on our backs and to gradually Croatise them." I believe I explained what this means in my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's clear now what is in the original language. One sentence is translated as two separate sentences. I don't think that's the problem, but that caused the confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yesterday you were shown a transcript from December of 1996 that had to do with the reintegration of Eastern Slavonia and how the Serbs -- what to do with the Serbs in that area. And there was discussion about buying their properties versus allowing them to return. Do you recall that general discussion?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that discussion from yesterday. But yesterday I wasn't aware that we spoke about Eastern Slavonia. Now you reminded me, because I remember some names from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to P466, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is a transcript from the 30th of August, 1995. And just a preliminary question: At this time, meaning the late August 1995, the only part of Croatia that had any substantial percentage of Serbs was Eastern Slavonia. Is that right? And if could you please answer with a yes or no, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were also other parts of Croatia, for example, the region around Delnice. The Serbs stayed there throughout the war as loyal citizens of Republic of Croatia, and they were majority population there, so my answer is no. Srpska Morovica [phoen] and the surrounding region, the Serbs had majority there throughout the aggression, and these Serbs were on the side of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if you could just briefly say what part of Croatia that area is, and roughly how many Serbs lived there at the time.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a region between Ogulin, northern side of the mountain Bijelo Lacica [phoen], there was about a dozen villages with several thousands Serbs who were majority there. I visited them at the time. I assisted in the reconstruction of an Orthodox monastery there after the war, and I know that they stayed there as loyal citizens of Croatia throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to page four of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S here. Now, Mr. Radic, you were not present at this meeting. I would just like to show you a short passage from it. It starts where Mr. Valentic is speaking. And that's at the bottom in the English. And here they're talking about the terms of a peaceful settlement in Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have the right page in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour. It's at the bottom of the page, Mr. Valentic speaking. At the top in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we get the remainder of the text in B/C/S on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, I believe it's at the top in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, now I see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Valentic says: "I do not know much about these problems, but I know from our department, because it is often mentioned that there is a big number of Serbs from Western Slavonia that live in the area of Baranja and Vukovar." And then someone says: "Around 30.000 of them." And he says: "So, it means that we should expect the request for their return to western Slavonia." And President Tudjman says: "That is a special problem, and we are going to concentrate on it." And if we go to the next page on the English Mr. Valentic says: "Yes, I am only warning you because I think this is one of important problems, as well as economic issues." And then President Tudjman says: "The next thing I wanted to say is that we should and we could put it like this - Serbs that come from Bosnia and from other places, they should leave." And someone says: "Yes." And Mr. Valentic says: "What, together with our Serbs?" And President Tudjman says: "Together with our Serbs, and we have to be very flexible about it because of the international community. We should suggest do replace them with" -- Sorry, this is the next page in the B/C/S. "We should suggest to replace them with Croats in Vojvodina and Serbia." And then someone says: "But we cannot write it down." And President Tudjman says: "What?" And Mr. Milas says: "Why? That option has been carried out always after the war." And then President Tudjman says: "Look, it is better not to complicate life for them and for us." And then Mr. Milas says: "That is a so-called option that exists in all international agreements after the First World War." Now, I understand you were not at this meeting, but as a member of the Croatian leadership and as someone deeply involved in demographic and population issues, I presume you were aware that the Croatian leadership was considering exchanging the Serbs in Eastern Slavonia for Croats in the Vojvodina and Serbia and conducting a population exchange. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. But having read this now, I believe that you've missed the point of this topic. Here they talked about Serbs who were not Croatian citizens and who could not become citizens of Croatia. They did not meet the conditions. So these were Serbs from Bosnia who came to the Danube region of Croatia. This is what is stated in the first sentence. So these are not Croatian citizens, and they had no conditions to apply to acquire the Croatian citizens. So this is my understanding, but I obviously have to make a reservation because I wasn't present at the meeting. In the first sentence somebody said what about Serb from Bosnia? So this was the point, the Serbs from Croatia stayed in Croatia. They are Croatian citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, if we could go to the previous page in the B/C/S. President Tudjman does say that: "We should put it like this, Serbs that came from Bosnia and from other places, they should leave." And then Mr. Valentic says: "What, together with our Serbs?" Now that reference to "our Serbs" can only mean a reference to Croatian Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present at the meeting, so I cannot comment on the detail, but I was here drawn to the fact that the President talked about Serbs who came there. But as I said, I wasn't present, so I do not have the full picture. But later on I was personally charged with reintegration of the Croatian Danube region. I was, myself, president of the commission for reintegration, and this is the only successful reintegration example worldwide, where the Serbs stayed and Croats came back. So when you asked me if I knew what -- that there was a plan to move them out, I know that there was no plan to move them out, but the plan was for them to stay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 4661, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, how much time your next topic take, approximately because we're at a point --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is the same topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same topic, yes. Because we have to take a break soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, this, Mr. Radic, is a transcript of a meeting you had with President Tudjman on the 28th of January, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 7 in the English and page 28 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And right at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, Mr. Radic, you say: "My logic in thinking this over is to find the quickest way of returning the Croats to Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "This is the question I have been asking myself, hence the idea was at what pace can we return the Croats?" And then if we go to the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, you say: "It would be good if we could issue written decisions in advance to the people that we wish to ... part of this is an idea that we force some of the residents of Posavina who will not be returning to Posavina, into that space, because I see no other way of placing it under our control but to ..." And then the President" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel, could you give us a page reference on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, it's the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And then the President says: "Or to exchange these Serbs for our Croats in Backa." Now Backa is an area in the Vojvodina in Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Backa is in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And here you and President Tudjman are discussing ways to increase the number of Croats and reduce the number of Serbs in Eastern Slavonia by, for example, forcing Bosnian Croats from the Posavina into that area, or exchanging Serbs in Eastern Slavonia for Croats in the Vojvodina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of this conversation that you read is that I note that I don't really expect that Croats would really return to that area, that native Croatians, those from Vukovar, would not be coming back in the same way that the Serbs from Vojnici would not be coming back. So we have empty apartments, and at the same time we have Croats from Posavina who are somewhere. It's better then for them to go to Vukovar than somewhere else. But on the margins, we're also referring to those people, those Serbs who do not wish to accept Croatian authority. We had that earlier when Croats from Backa and Srijem exchanged their homes with Serbs from Western Slavonia. This was not something that was encouraged by us, but this was something that was initiated on their part. I know many examples of Serbs, even from Zadar, who were JNA officers and had lovely houses in Zadar. They escaped from Croatia not during Storm but before. They came to Vojvodina, and then they exchanged houses with the Croats in Vojvodina. They moved to Vojvodina, and the Croats went to Zadar, for example. But this was before the peaceful reintegration. I told the President, on the basis of facts, my concerns that many Croats who spent eight years being as displaced persons in Zagreb would not want to go back to Vukovar but would stay in Zagreb because they already had jobs in Zagreb, their children were going to school. This was something that happened in large numbers. It was not individual during the war, another life happens, where then preconditions are created for a person not to come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to go back to an earlier part of your answer. You said you knew plenty examples of Serbs, for example, from Zadar, who had lovely houses in Zadar, they escaped from Croatia, they came to Vojvodina, and then they exchanged houses with the Croats. But President Tudjman here isn't talking about people who have already left the areas that they lived in, exchanging houses. He is talking about exchanging people; right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What he is talking is that we had the experience from five years before, or three years before, that, when the Croatian came into power, the person who was in the JNA or somewhere, they're not going to stay in Croatia. They left Zadar, they left Vojnic, and they would also leave Vukovar. This is what we're talking about. Once we establish power, we know. We have the experience. Persons like that left before and they're going to go any way. So if they're going to go, it would be better to have them exchange their property, then have this peaceful reintegration. We were talking about empty properties -- well, look, all the policemen in Croatia were Serbs. I don't know ten Croat policemen in Croatia. So most of them left. Not all of them, but many of them were brought there from other areas. They're not natives, and we're not even referring to the JNA here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. This is a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For scheduling purposes, I would like to invite the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'll have a break, and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, as far as time is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I need about another 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 20 minutes. Yes, that makes it approximately the two sessions, as you announced. If you could save a bit more time, that would be appreciated, but you will not take much time after the break. We'll have a break and resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could look at P2536, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, the document that's about to come on your screen is a text of a speech that President Tudjman gave in Vukovar, at the Vukovar railway station, on the 8th of June, 1997. And according to the text, there was a Croatian government delegation there. Do you happen to recall now whether you were present at this speech?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 4 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. And this is the first full paragraph in the B/C/S, and it's the third paragraph in the English that begins: "Ladies and gentlemen ..." And President Tudjman says: "Ladies and gentlemen, all those Serbs who are citizens of Croatia, who have taken Croatian citizenship and who are living in this county and the neighbouring Osijek-Baranja county, and the entire Danubian area, if they want to return to their homes in western parts of Croatia from Pakrac to Knin, they will be allowed to return. About 14.500 have already returned. If they do not want to return, we shall give them compensation so that they can go wherever they wish." "Out of humanitarian reasons Croatia will resolve individual cases of Serbs who fled Croatia, despite the fact that I, as president, personally invited them to stay. Out of humanitarian reasons we will resolve their cases so they can return to Croatia to rejoin their families. "Of course, there can be no question of 200.000 or 150.000 people returning, because then we would again have conflict and war. Nobody in the world can force us to do that. "In any case, they themselves - 90 per cent of them - do not wish to return. But such is history. After World War II around one and a half million people - those so-called [sic] Turks and Muslims - left this region for turkey, and around 1 million Greeks went to Greece, and so on. "Following World War II over 12 million people have been displaced throughout Europe. Not every evil is wholly evil. Out of every evil, some good may come. So, let us, first of all, create conditions for a peaceful life for the Croatian people, the Serb and other ethnic communities in Croatia. Let us create conditions for normalisation of good-neighbourly relations between Croatia and Serbia and Yugoslavia along the lines of - as I wrote 20 years ago - Scandinavisation of the area based on mutual recognition of nations and mutual respect, and then ethnic minorities will enjoy complete freedom and quality." When President Tudjman says there is no question of 200.000 or 150.000 people returning, he is referring to the Croatian Serbs living outside Croatia at that time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is saying that there is no likelihood that all of the 150.000 people would come back, because a large number among them is of people who were directly connected to the aggression on Croatia. He is aware that those who were commanding or participated in the aggression against Croatia would not return. I mean, this is realistic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, you've gone beyond the question that I asked, so please focus on answering just the specific question. So when he says -- and when he says: "There's no question of these Croatian Serbs returning, because then we would again have conflict and war," that reflects his view that it would result in a strategic threat to Croatia if these people were allowed to return; right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. If the officers of the JNA would return, of course, we would be threatened. I don't see anything that would be disputable then. He said that some people would return. 15.000 or so. But not all of them, first of all, because they did not wish to return, and, secondly, because we did not wish for the aggressors to come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, again there is a translation issue, and I apologise to Ms. Gustafson, but there's a word that the witness is using that is not in the English translation but is in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's right before the 150 or 200.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. In the original text it -- translation of the text? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The original is the English just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The original is the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that President Tudjman spoke in Croatian, so I don't know ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right, but this text came from an English report, and we translated into Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then we would have to check exactly, because this is it precisely the dilemma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- could you point at where the difference, in your view, is, Mr. Misetic. Because if it is not a problem between Croatian and English, then it may be a problem between English and Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In Croatian it says: "We cannot talk anymore about all 150 or 200.000 returning." And in the English it says: "We cannot talk about 150 to 200.000 returning." I think there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I apologise, I believe that these are both originals. We found them separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both originals. So then we have a problem, because nowhere in the bottom it says that the authoritative is -- Okay. That is on the record, now, that we are looking at two different versions and which one refers to return of all, and then the number, whereas the other does not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now just going back to an answer you just give, Mr. Radic. You said: "He said that some people would return, 15.000 or so." Was that number 15.000, was that a number that was considered an acceptable number for return?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It would have been better if more people were to have returned. At that time I was the minister for returns, so it would have been better for more people to return. But, obviously, it was necessary for the conditions to ripen and to be created for larger numbers of people to return. I personally would not be happy with 14 or 15.000 only returning. I would prefer for this figure to be bigger.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So when you referred to the number 15.000, that wasn't your view, that was a number President Tudjman used; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I quoted what President Tudjman said at the time in Vukovar, and he said 14.500. You're asking me to comment on the President Tudjman's speech which he gave. I didn't give any speech at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, let me tell you how I at least understand this line. About 14 and a half thousand have already returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I was referring to an answer the witness gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if that's the case, that was unclear to me, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if it was clear to everyone, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Radic, when President Tudjman talks about 12 million people being displaced after World War II and then says out of every evil some good may come, he's referring to the population displacements after World War II as a good that came out of the evil of that war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman is a historian; I'm an engineer. I cannot really comment on these historical numbers and theories.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Fair enough. And yesterday you were asked questions by the Chamber on this general topic, and you said that you wanted as large a number of people to return as possible, and you said that this included Serbs and that increasingly reached the conclusion that the correct thing to do was to offer everyone to return. Now, at this time, in June of 1997, it was not the view of the leadership that everyone should return, or that the -- it was not the view of the leadership that all the Croatian Serbs outside of Croatia should return, and that is reflected by President Tudjman's speech; right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, with the explanation that, in order for somebody to return, at least two steps have to be made, accept Croatian citizenship, become a Croatian citizen, and to submit a request for return. Return is a question of free will. It's not something that can be a result of force. We cannot force somebody to return. They have to take Croatian citizenship and submit a request to return. Out of this 150 to 200.000 do not wish or did not wish to be Croatian citizens. They don't want that still today, 15 years after these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber has heard quite a bit of evidence -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, we are moving further and further away from what was the -- the subject matter of the examination-in-chief. We focussed very much on what was said, especially in 1995. Not to say that we heard a bit about later developments, but several times, the Chamber said, What happened afterwards is a different matter than what was discussed in mid and late 1995. Now, we are not only looking at what happened later but also on what was said at that time. Some of the matters, I mean, individual or mass return, having dealt with already quite considerably and where, apparently, this witness has -- I wouldn't say no knowledge but limited knowledge, and it certainly moves away further and further from what the Chamber had on its mind. Do you have any other questions which brings us closer again --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would like to move to the 8th -- sorry, 11th August 1995 VONS meeting, which is P2673.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you said you would need approximately 20 minutes. Would that be your last topic?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Two brief topics, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please try to do it as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 20 in the English and page 47 in the B/C/S -- oh, sorry, I apologise. We've uploaded a full English translation. I'm not sure if it has been linked into e-court. The doc ID of the full English translation is 01870803 -- 0187-0803-ET-1. If that could be brought up alongside the B/C/S. And if we could have page 47 in the B/C/S, which should be 12 pages before this one. And page 20 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, and pardon me if I'm behind here. But I only get a 17-page document, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that Ms. Gustafson just referred to a full translation having been uploaded, and that's what she's dealing with now. Is that correctly understood, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I hope so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is at least what is on her mind, whether what is on our screen is the what on her mind is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the spirit of trying to follow along, it's just a bit difficult, and maybe I could just -- excuse me. I'm going to get the assistance of our Case Manager.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We need to go back 12 pages in the B/C/S. It should be page 47, but I'm not ... I may have made a mistake. There we go. And if we could move to the bottom in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, this is you speaking right after Operation Storm on the 11th of August --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel, I'm sorry. I don't mean to interrupt. What page are we talking about in the English? I have this uploaded, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's the 20th page. There are a number of different page numbers at the bottom of the page because it's a number of different pieces of different translations, it was disclosed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on our screen now. And it's page 8 in the hard copy version, which allows you to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Here, Mr. Radic, you're talking about the fact that: "The full effect of Operations Flash and Storm is that expelled persons are returning to their homes, 120.000 persons, Croats from those areas are still expelled persons." And in the next paragraph, you talk about a detailed analysis aimed at creating conditions as soon as possible for returns. And if we go to the next page in the English, you discuss three waves of Croats to return. The first wave will be those places where houses have remained intact, houses of Croats that had been settled by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we go to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we on the right page in English? I think the hard copy -- yes, now we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And then you talk about the second surge. And that's at the bottom of the page and moving to the next page in the B/C/S. And that's Croats returning to liberated apartments and houses in areas near to where their destroyed houses are. And about halfway through that paragraph, you talk about the third group, the third wave, which is return to those villages or small Croatian towns that were totally destroyed, such as Sveti Rok, Lovinac, Saborsko, et cetera. And if we go to the next page in the B/C/S and the bottom of the page in English, you're speaking again. And in the next page in the English, right after you refer again to Lovinac and Sveti Rok, you ask that there be a meeting in a small group to agree precisely what places it will be, what points in a strategic sense to fill with people in the coming days. And you say: "It is most urgent, most important in places where the return can take place in a month at the most." And you talk about beginning instruction in schools. Now, here you describe these three waves of Croats that will be returned to these liberated areas as urgently as possible. And the Chamber has heard evidence that quite a number of Croats did start moving into these areas quite soon after Operation Storm. So my question is: Were you successful, were you able to move in quite a number of Croats in these three categories as quickly as you indicated that you aimed to do in this transcript?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not even close.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, in a transcript that you were shown the other day of the 5th of October government session, the one that was in the binder that you took, you said that you been able to settle 8.000 Croats in the areas of Vojnic and Vrginmost. Is that an example of you achieving some results in this area of returning people to the area after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one example where we had settled displaced persons from Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was actually doing my best to give you a shorter answer, but now you're evidently looking for an explanation. The programme of return was proceeding much slower than we envisioned that -- a week after Storm in an ideal enthusiastic kind of situation, as expected, that a person who had spent a few years away form his home, in some hotel or another apartment, couldn't wait for the moment to return to his home. But I saw that this was not like that, because those five years of living somewhere else created many new circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Are you able to recall now approximately how many thousands of Croats you had been able to bring back into the area by, for example, the 5th of October, when you referred to the Croats in Vojnic and Vrginmost.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember that. But I remember well that, at the end of the government's term of office, after five years of working we said that we had managed to return 200.000 people to their homes, that we had created the conditions and restored or reconstructed the homes for that number of people. But I really cannot remember the exact figures for that period, for which period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all the question I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I would, just as a housekeeping matter, ask that this full translation be replaced for the one in e-court, and I also neglected to tender 65 ter 4661.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I take it that's the newspaper article; is that right? I take that back. It's a presidential transcript of January 28th.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, leave is granted to replace an incomplete translation by the complete translation in relation to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2673? That leave is granted. Could you please assign a number to 65 ter 4661.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2714. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Radic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Mr. Kehoe, first of all, we have to conclude today five minutes earlier than normal. Would you please keep that in mind. Would you please also keep in mind that from the examination by the Chamber and then by the cross-examination, it turns out that on various matters that the same issues arise again, and what the Chamber would like that avoid is that by taking another approach, we end up with the same answers which would then primarily emphasise that from whatever point of view you look at it, you would get similar answers, and I think that the Defence should avoid that. We're here not to emphasise the answers we've already heard, but, rather, to have the evidence primarily tested within the guide-lines the Chamber gave for cross-examination of Chamber witnesses. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you, and in that vein, I'll use a Latin expression "festina lente." And I will try to move quickly but not too quickly and avoid topics that have come up before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In Greek it is speude bradeos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I never took Greek, Judge, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radic. I would like to cover some topics, and as the President just said we're not going to repeat everything we did in the past. But I would like, for one moment, to contextualise some of these conversations. And I'm talking about the conversations that began with you and President Tudjman and others immediately after Operation Storm. We've seen some discussion on 462 both yesterday and today which took place just days after Storm, 11 August 1995. But I would like do put into context a series of events and your mindset, at least, in talking to President Tudjman as to what you're talking about at that particular time. Now this morning you had mentioned that you had had some experience as a result of Operation Flash and the situation in Western Slavonia, going back to May/June of 1995. Now, in Western Slavonia, there was in fact a large element of the Serb population who voluntarily left Western Slavonia after Operation Flash, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. So here in front of us we have the minutes from one or two meetings, but in those days, I personally spoke to President Tudjman for at least 20 times concerning different topics. You are mentioning the situation in Western Slavonia, but we can also say that many Serbs left other parts of Croatia as soon as Croatia proclaimed independence. I believe as many as 20.000 Serbs left Zagreb in the period after the proclamation of independence because they simply could not accept Croatia as their country, as their state. So we spoke about the overall context of all the events that happened during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I would like to focus our attention, at least initially, on the experience of the Republic of Croatia in Western Slavonia, prior to Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if could I bring up on the screen 65 ter 520, which is a report of the Security Council dated 9 June 1995. Excuse me, 65 ter 520. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As you can see -- just waiting for the B/C/S. As you can see, Mr. Radic, it is a UN report. And I would like to turn to the fourth page in the English, which begins -- and third page in the B/C/S which begins with the heading: Sector West. And in that area, in the end of the first paragraph I will begin to read their analysis of the UN which notes that: "... the Croatian government has sought to encourage Serbs to remain in the sector and has issued personal documents, including citizenship papers and some passports to those who have applied for them." Paragraph 15: "Despite the evident efforts of the Croatian government to achieve high standards of respect for the Serbs' human rights in Sector West and to discourage them from moving into Bosnia-Herzegovina, an atmosphere of fear prevails, and only a few hundred are likely to choose to stay in the sector." Now that ultimately became the reality, that Serbs in an enterprise called Operation Safe Passage, left the area under the auspices of the UN. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll offer into evidence 65 ter 520.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that this is an UN report from about this time in evidence already with a D number. I can double-check. I'm not sure if it's this one, though. But there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think, if I may, there is a Mazowiecki report in that -- is about that time-frame, and this is a different report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, his document shall be assigned Exhibit D2020. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2020 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let us go to post-Operation Storm where -- where President Tudjman is talking to international leaders about the likelihood of Serbs returning, and I want to show you a series of documents before I ask you this, and I do think if we move through this expeditiously, we can finish this area before we have to leave for the day. And the first conversation I would like to talk to you about is P449, which is a minutes of a meeting on the 18th of August, 1995, with the President and Ambassador Holbrooke of the United States, General Clark of the United States, as well as Ambassador Galbraith. And if I might just have one moment to get the pagination on this correctly -- correct, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The reason the pagination is off a bit, Mr. President, is that there was a portion of this that was initially put into evidence and then another portion of it was tagged on thereafter. So the pagination at the bottom of the pages doesn't necessarily equate to what it is in e-court. It is page 33 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me read to you at the top of the page. And this is 17 in English. Let me read you the comment by Ambassador Holbrooke, and I will tell you at the top of this page in the B/C/S is -- this is Ambassador Holbrooke speaking to the President. And he says: "If you could just bring those people back, if could you hold a speech and say that the war is over, to return, most of them will not return. But tell them to return, emphasise it. At least mention that they should return. President Tudjman: "I would be very content if about 10 per cent of them returned." Ambassador Holbrooke: "All right, tell them to return. Give them compensation ..." Now, the last document that I'd just like to refer to before I ask you a few questions is Ambassador Galbraith's diary, which is P459, and this is for the entry on September the 15th. And in English, it should be in e-court 46 of 76.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, P458. It is the fifth tab in B/C/S. Tab number 5 in B/C/S. And page 46 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that's not the right page, Mr. President, bit if I can just read it in English and we can just move along, because I'm just going to read a sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In his diary, Ambassador Galbraith recounts a conversation with Mr. Sarinic. And in his diary, he said he notes that he told

utterances.speaker: MR. SARINIC
utterances.text: "I also noted that not many would want to return, at most 20 per cent." Now, the conversation with Ambassador Holbrooke, a public conversation with an ambassador of another country, he is -- President Tudjman is talking about 10 per cent coming back, and Ambassador Galbraith is talking about 20 per cent coming back. Now, in these conversations that the government was having with Ambassador Galbraith and with other international leaders, did anyone, any of these international leaders suggest to you, given the fact that 80 per cent were not going return, what the Republic of Croatia was supposed to do with all this vacant property?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if a foundation could be laid as to this witness's contacts with international leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, you in fact asked questions about international leaders having some influence in changing the Law on the Temporary Takeover of Property from 30 to 90 days, et cetera, and I certainly would ask this witness if he knows directly, in conversations with international leaders or in conversations with Croatian leaders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we are talking about -- primarily about the international community, but that -- let me just see ... Until now, you have referred to the conversation with Ambassador Galbraith. If there are any others you have on your mind, please specify. If not, we could invite the witness to ask whether he is aware of any discussions with other international leaders on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you answer the President's question in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of this information, that high representatives of the United States were under the impression that not more than 20 per cent were to return. I also personally met with many ambassadors at the time who shared similar opinion. Their judgement was that not more than that number were to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With that number in mind, that equates to 80 per cent of the Serb population not coming back. Now, in conversations with these international leaders, did they ever explain to you what the Republic of Croatia was supposed to do with property owned by 80 per cent of the Serbs who were not going to come back and who was going to live in these areas?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was somewhat different, because they allowed us to offer our solution, our proposal, and then they -- they supported it. For many of them it was acceptable that we suggested that the property would be best preserved if we gave it for temporary use, in a way in which we explained already in this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, the first conversation that we talked to you about was the minutes held at the Presidential Palace where there -- and this is in P462. We don't need to bring up right now. I'm sure you recall that conversation. And it's a conversation with the President, with you, with minister Susak, with Prime Minister Valentic that took place on 11th of August. But that conversation that takes place on 11th August is -- that conversation concerning the temporary takeover law is being conducted with the belief of the parties that the Serb population is not going to come back. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, that's right. From the first moment, we had this impression which was furthermore supported by the representatives of the international community, such as you mentioned yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So this conversation not a conversation in the context of keeping the Serb population out, but, rather, The Serb population is not going to come back. What are we going to do with this property, all this vacant property, especially in light of the security concerns with the ongoing war against the combined Serb forces. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely right. Even the conversation that I had with the President on the 22nd of August, starts with me saying, President, we have to preserve the properties. And he say, Yes, of course, we have to preserve all the properties in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic. We have to break off now, pursuant to the President's instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Radic, I give you the same instructions as I gave to you yesterday, that is, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony whether already given yesterday and today or still to be given tomorrow. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00, although in Courtroom III. We adjourn, and we resume on -- one second. The question was put to you whether you would keep the folders. If you would like to keep them, if you would want to re-read what is in there, that's fine. If you would rather say, Let's not lose it, I'll give it back to the Tribunal, then we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that score, is it possible - again this is a large transcript of P464 that Ms. Gustafson went through - if there's no objections to any parties of giving a copy in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, apparently. I'm looking at Ms. Gustafson who is nodding no objection. Then this can be -- in the appropriate way be given to the witness. We will resume tomorrow, Friday, the 26th of February, 9.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 26th day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.,
